 Public Comment: The public is encouraged to address City Council on any matter listed on the agenda or on any other matter within its
 jurisdiction subject to the rules of decorum described in Section 2.08.020 of the Norwalk Municipal Code. If you wish to address City
 Council, please complete the card that is provided at the rear entrance to Council Chambers and hand the card to the Sergeant at Arms.
 City Council will hear public comment on items listed on the agenda during discussion of the matter and prior to a vote. City Council will
 hear public comment on matters not listed on the agenda during the Oral Communications period.

 Pursuant to provisions of the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the agenda, or unless certain emergency
 or special circumstances exist. The City Council may direct staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a
 future City Council meeting.

 Please adhere to the following procedures when addressing the City Council:
   Comments should be limited to 3 minutes or less.
   Comments should be directed to the City Council as a whole and not directed to individual Councilmembers.

 Americans with Disabilities Act: In compliance with the ADA, if you need special assistance to participate in a City meeting or other
 services offered by this City, please contact the City Clerk’s department, (562) 929-5720. Assisted listening devices are available at this
 meeting. Ask the City Clerk if you desire to use this device. Upon request, the agenda and documents in the agenda packet can be
 made available in appropriate alternative formats to persons with a disability. Notification of at least 48 hours prior to the meeting or time
 when services are needed will assist the City staff in assuring that reasonable arrangements can be made to provide accessibility to the
 meeting or service.

 Note: Any writings and/or documents provided to a majority of the City Council regarding any item on this agenda after it has been posted will also
 be made available for public inspection.

 Writings and/or documents are available for inspection in the City Clerk’s Department, City Hall, 12700 Norwalk Boulevard during regular business
 hours, 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., Monday – Thursday and 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., every other Friday; telephone (562) 929-5720. You may also contact the

CLOSED SESSION REPORT

The Deputy City Attorney reported that there was no reportable action taken on Item Nos.
I and II, however, indicated No. II is also on the regular agenda as Item No. 12. She
reported that City Council voted to join the litigation by a 5-0 vote for Item No. III; and
during discussion on Item No. IV City Council voted 5-0 to approve not opting out of the
class action lawsuit.

CITY COUNCIL COMMENTS

City Council expressed appreciation for the success of the Halloween Parade.
Councilmember Ayala thanked all staff for making the 38th Arturo Sanchez Jr. Halloween
Parade a huge success that was well attended. Councilmember Ramirez shared that
pledge of allegiance participant Rick Ramirez participates in many City events; and
requested Mr. Rodriguez, Grand Marshal of the parade, be invited to a future City Council
meeting to be recognized for his participation. Councilmember Perez highlighted
upcoming events such as the Pumpkin Float event being held at the Norwalk Aquatic
Pavilion October 20, Halloween at the Hargitt House October 21, and the Halloween
Festival October 27 at Norwalk, Hermosillo, and Lakeside parks; shared that the Chamber
of Commerce hosted their Annual Norwalk Chamber Fall Festival in October and thanked
all who attended; encouraged residents to participate in all the Halloween events being
held at Social Services and Senior Center; thanked First Responders, Public Safety,
Sheriffs, Homeless Operations Prevention and Engagement team (HOPE), and Code
Compliance for all they do. Vice Mayor Rios reported on her attendance at the Greater
Los Angeles County Vector Control Meeting, the Miniachis De Norwalk performance at

Background:

The City has contracted for professional services with Bucknam and Associates Inc. (Bucknam)

Bucknam has assisted staff with the development of improvement plans to upgrade the City’s
utilities infrastructure, consultation support and applications for federal and state grant
opportunities to fund various utility projects; utility programs management and technical
engineering support for the improvements to the City’s utilities systems. The City currently has
several active and ongoing utility capital improvement projects, funding applications, and
pending agreements with other water purveyors utilizing Bucknam’s involvement.

In October of 2021, the City’s Well No. 10 began to exceed the maximum levels Title 22 of the
California Code of Regulations (State drinking water standards) allows for Benzene. Benzene
has been on the State’s Primary Volatile Organic Carbons (VOC) contaminant list for
groundwater since 1989 and is both natural and man-made. Examples of man-made Benzene
use is as a constituent in motor fuels and in the manufacture of detergents, pharmaceuticals,
and dyes. In order to meet State drinking water standards, the City will need to treat groundwater
from Well No. 10 to remove Benzene by implementing a treatment system.

In May of 2023, City Council approved an agreement with Civiltec Engineering, Inc. (Civiltec) to
provide on-call professional engineering services for the Well No. 10 treatment system. The
scope of work for Civiltec includes design, environmental compliance, bidding process support,
construction engineering support, project startup and commissioning, and project close out

Background:

In 2011, a group of cities/agencies, also known as watershed “Permittees,” including the City of
Norwalk created a Technical Committee to prepare an Implementation Plan, Monitoring Plan,
and special studies for the Coyote Creek and San Gabriel River Reach 1 cities, as required by
the Regional Water Quality Control Board (Regional Board). The watershed group entered into
a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Gateway Water Management Authority
(GWMA). The GWMA has been the acting administrator for the group, per the MOU, as of June
2012. Funds were collected and expended for the Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL) work.

In May 2013, the TMDL Committee plus additional representatives of cities/agencies in the San
Jose Creek Reach 2 and Reach 3 of the San Gabriel River changed the name of the TMDL
Committee. The new Lower San Gabriel River Watershed (LSGR) Committee name was to
reflect the expanded duties and members. The newly formed LSGR Committee began to work
together to meet the requirements under the Regional Board, Los Angeles Region, National
Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System
Permit Order No. R4-2012-0175 (MS4 Permit).

GMWA Board Representation
Per the MOU, each city/agency is represented by one primary Board Member and up to three
alternates on the GWMA Board. In accordance with to GWMA’s Bylaws adopted on October 12,
2015, all non-Legislative Body appointments to the GWMA Board must be done by

Resolution. GWMA Board Members and alternate Board Members serve two-year terms
beginning October 1st of each odd-numbered year and concluding on September 30th two years
later. Resolution No. 23-65 would designate a Board Member and alternate Board Member(s)
to serve continuously across successive two-year terms such that the governing body need not
re-appoint the same persons to the GWMA Board every two years, unless the governing body
desires to change its designated Board Member and/or alternate Board Member or must
otherwise fill a vacancy. The City has vacancies for Board Member and Alternate Members.

Agreement with GWMA for Harbor Toxic Pollutants TMDLs
The United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) via the Clean Water Act assists
states, territories, and authorized tribes in listing impaired waters and developing TMDLs for
these waterbodies. A TMDL establishes the maximum amount of a pollutant allowed in a
waterbody and serves as the starting point or planning tool for restoring water quality.

The USEPA established the TMDL for Toxic Pollutants on March 23, 2012, with the intent of
protecting and improving water quality in the Dominguez Channel and the Greater Los Angeles
and Long Beach Harbor Waters (Harbor Toxic Pollutants TMDL). The Harbor Toxic Pollutants
TMDL regulates certain discharges from NPDES MS4 permit holders (MS4 Permitees) requiring
organization and cooperation among the group.

The MS4 Permitees are the cities of Artesia, Bell, Bell Gardens, Bellflower, Cerritos, Commerce,
Compton, Cudahy, Downey, Hawaiian Gardens, Huntington Park, La Mirada, Lakewood, Long
Beach, Lynwood, Maywood, Montebello, Norwalk, Paramount, Pico Rivera, Santa Fe Springs,
Signal Hill, South Gate, Vernon, Whittier, Water Replenishment District, Central Basin Municipal
Water District, Port of Long Beach, and the Long Beach Water Department.

MS4 Permittees desired to achieve the objectives of the Harbor Toxic Pollutants TMDL. In 2018,
they executed an additional agreement, separate from the MOU, with the GWMA to install a
monitoring station in the Los Angeles River at Wardlow Road, monitoring station in the San
Gabriel River near Spring Street, and monitoring station in the Coyote Creek, also near Spring
Street. These monitoring stations will ensure consistency with other regional monitoring
programs and usability with other TMDL related studies. The 2018 agreement also covered
maintenance of the monitoring stations and administrative coordination for the various MS4
Permittees by GWMA. The 2018 original agreement with GWMA expired in June of 2023.

impacted for concrete restoration are completed. The remaining construction items to complete
are the roadway pavement, valve cover and manhole grade adjustments, and pavement

City Streets Improvements

Typically, water main projects only involve the replacement of the affected pavement section
above the new water main trench. Water main projects do not replace pavement beyond the
affected section unless under special circumstances and where appropriate funding sources are
used. Total costs for Project No. 7442 include pavement restoration work previously part of and
funded by Project No. 7926.

Construction for Project No. 7926 was scheduled to start before Project No. 7442. Since water
main construction would disturb the newly paved streets, resurfacing of those streets was moved
to Project No. 7442 for logistical reasons (Attachment 2).

Grind and overlay was the original roadway resurface method for the above streets. Resurfacing
of these streets includes only the pavement surface section. However, it was discovered during
water main construction that the roadway structural section was in poor condition on 162nd, 163rd
and 164th Streets. The structural sections for these streets requires replacement before
paving. Had these streets remained in Project No. 7926, the substandard structural sections
would require replacement. (Attachment 2)

Proper rehabilitation requires removal and replacement of the structural sections to insure proper
pavement performance and service life. Fortunately, only these three streets require full depth
reclamation to restore the roadway pavement. Total estimated additional costs for 162nd, 163rd
and 164th Streets is $350,000. Proposition C funding would be appropriated for the streets
resurfacing work to be added to Project No. 7442.

The intersection of 166th Street and Pioneer Boulevard is also within the Project No. 7442
limits. Part of the project improvements installed a new fire hydrant through the intersection to
provide enhanced fire protection for this area. The intersection pavement requires resurfacing
and requires the crosswalks to be brought up to the current “continental crosswalk”
standard. Doing this work now offers benefit of both improved logistics and reduced costs under
a current contract with the same work type when compared to if the work were done under a
separate contract. In addition, the southerly half of intersection is within the City of Artesia’s
jurisdiction. Staff discussed the additive work with the City of Artesia and they agreed with both
the benefits and logistics, and are very interested in participating with the intersection
improvements. The estimated cost for this work is $111,500. Proposition C funds would be

AUTHORITY
 Section 65855 of the California Government Code states that the Planning Commission shall
make a written recommendation on the adoption or amendment of the Zoning Ordinance.

Section 17.02.260.D of the NMC stipulates that the Planning Commission render its
recommendation on a Zoning Text Amendment, including the reasons for the recommendation,
to the City Council.

Section 17.02.290.D requires a written recommendation of approval by the Planning
Commission to City Council for Zone Change applications.

INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND

The Automobile Parking (P) zone was adopted by Ordinance No. 114 in 1959 with the intent
to serve as setbacks/buffers for incompatible uses. There are 275 parcels that contain a P
zoning either exclusively or within the parcel. The P zoning primarily prohibits construction of
a building; however, 43 existing sites contain structures.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION

The request consists of Zoning Text Amendment No. 2023-01 to amend various sections of
Title 17 of the NMC as it relates to the P zone and Zone Change No. 2023-01 to remove the
P zone from the zoning map.

The proposed update will simplify the list of permitted land uses and zones, minimize conflicts
between zoning code requirements, and serve as a proactive approach of enhancing economic
development.

ANALYSIS

A key objective of the proposed project is to expand development opportunities throughout the
city. The project will allow property owners to build on respective parcels, while still conforming
to requirements such as setbacks and building height. Additionally, it will remove redundant
provisions that are outdated from current conditions and that conflict with goals to increase
economic development. Recently approved projects, such as the Alondra-Maidstone mixed-
use development and the Rosecrans-Norwalk commercial building are examples of vacant
 sites that remained dormant for a long time and were difficult to redevelop due to the P zone.
Summarized below are proposed changes to the Zoning Code and Zoning Map.

Zoning Text Amendment

To simplify the code, staff proposes to delete the Automobile Parking (P) zoning and related
provisions. The P zoning significantly hinders development, where other design features and
code standards can apply and allow for development in a responsible manner. In consideration
that the P zoning created a buffer between potential incompatible development, a minimum
five feet setback and maximum 35 feet building height are imposed to provide protections to
adjacent residential zones. New development proposed to reduce the minimum setback or
exceed the maximum building height would be subject to review and approval of a conditional
use permit.

Zone Change

Of the total 275 parcels that will be affected by the zone change, 52 parcels will completely
revert to either residential (41) or commercial (11) zoning to match the underlying General Plan
land use designation, and 223 parcels will remove the partial P zoning buffer, which is 15 to
50 feet wide, and revert to the corresponding zoning. The 223 split zoned parcels will be re-
designated as follows: 34.08% (76 parcels) as residential, 40.77% (95 parcels) as industrial,
20.18% (45 parcels) as commercial, and the remaining 3.14% (7 parcels) as open space or
specific plan. The ZC will encourage development by expanding developable area on the sites
and providing the property owner more development opportunities. Consistency between the
zoning map and General Plan land use map will occur as a result of this proposed project.

Public Notification

Notice of this public hearing was published in The Norwalk Patriot and posted at the City’s
three designated posting sites and the City website on September 14, 2023. All 3,444 property
owners within 300 feet of impacted parcels were also notified.

ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT
 The project is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to
CEQA Guidelines Section 15061(b)(3). The project will not involve any construction nor have
a significant effect on the environment.

SUMMARY

The proposed ZTA and ZC involve removing the Automobile Parking zone and related
provisions from the Norwalk Municipal Code, and corresponding zone on the City Zoning Map.
With the amendments, development opportunities will expand consistent with the General
Plan, conflicts between zoning code requirements will be minimized, and the list of permitted
uses and zones will be simplified. Staff recommends that the Planning Commission
recommend approval of the project to City Council.

INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND

The Precise Development Plan (PDP) requirement was adopted by Ordinance No. 757 in
1972 and intended to achieve a reasonable level of quality in harmony with precise plans and
community objectives for social, economic and physical well-being, and to protect existing
and potential developments and uses on adjacent and surrounding properties. A precise
development plan involves a set of plans conforming to the zoning code that is subject to
review and approval by the Planning Commission. It does not grant provisions to deny any

is prompted with new construction or the relocation of structures in any zone other than
single-family residences and accessory buildings in residential zones.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION

The request consists of Zoning Text Amendment No. 2023-02 to amend various sections of
Title 17 of the NMC to streamline the PDP process. It will serve as a proactive approach of
enhancing economic development and encouraging a positive image of the City.

ANALYSIS

The project will expedite the PDP application by reducing the associated processing time and
changing the reviewing authority to the Community Development Director. With PDPs, the
review primarily involves checking site plans, floor plans, and elevations in conformance with
development standards in the NMC and ensuring compatibility with the neighborhood. In
converting to an administrative process, the PDP will encourage the redevelopment of vacant
properties, create more opportunities for employment and goods and services, and promote
a positive image of the development process in Norwalk. Even with a streamlined process,
the proposed amendment will allow the Community Development Director to refer a project to
the Planning Commission for discretionary action. Additionally, if a PDP were submitted
concurrently with a discretionary application, such as a conditional use permit, both
applications would be subject to review and approval by the Planning Commission. Review
by the Director will apply to projects that are permitted in the zone, conform to development
standards in the NMC, and solely require a PDP.

Background:

For many years, City Council has supported energy efficiency upgrades to buildings and
infrastructure. Staff have completed energy audits and implemented numerous energy
efficiency projects to upgrade facilities which provide energy efficient buildings, a comfortable
environment for visitors and staff, and overall cost savings for the City. Projects have included
light-emitting diode (LED) lighting retrofits, upgrades to heating, ventilation, and air conditioning
(HVAC) units, plumbing fixtures to save water, and a variety of other projects.

To build on these efforts, this City has been working with Syserco Energy Solutions (SES), a
qualified energy services company, to identify energy conservation measures and renewable
energy opportunities. SES has analyzed the City’s energy use data, surveyed the City’s facilities
and equipment, modeled buildings for performance, identified opportunities to utilize resources
more efficiently, developed energy conservation measures (ECMs), and calculated potential
energy savings from the implementation of the proposed measures.

Energy conservation measures identified include the following:

 Install solar panel arrays at several facilities
 Install energy efficient “cool” roofs at Transportation/Public Services facility buildings
 Install building management system thermostats at several facilities
 Retrofit ballfield lighting at Holifield and Zimmerman parks to LED
 Install ballfield lighting at Lakeside and Ramona parks
 Replace HVAC units more than 18 years old
 Refurbish all other HVAC units to provide protective polyurethane coating

 Replace transformer at City Hall to a high efficiency unit
 Building exterior upgrades to add and/or replace door sweeps and sealing of doors

California Government Code Section 4217.12 (CA 4217) provides that a public agency may
enter into an energy services contract on such terms as the City Council determines are in the
best interest of the City provided City Council conducts a public hearing and can make the
following finding:

  1. The anticipated cost to the City for energy or conservation services provided under the
  contract will be less than the anticipated marginal cost to the City of the energy that would
  have been consumed in the absence of these purchases.

  2. That the difference, if any, between the fair rental value for the real property subject to
  the facility ground lease and the agreed rent, is anticipated to be offset by below-market
  energy purchases or other benefits provided under the energy service contract.

In other words, CA GC 4217 allows the City to directly engage a qualified energy services
company in a design-build agreement provided that the energy cost savings that result from the
agreement are greater than the cost of the improvements.

The proposed energy services contract with SES calculates that the total energy savings, over
the expected useful life of the equipment is $39,458,180. These savings come from energy
savings that result from more efficient equipment, savings from buying less electricity from
Southern California Edison and instead generating electricity via on-site solar panels and
operational savings from reduced maintenance of old equipment.

Staff is requesting that the City enter into a contract with SES for the sustainability, energy
efficiency, and facility improvement project. Tax-exempt bond financing by private placement
or public offering for the project will be secured and brought back to City Council for approval at
a later date.

Fiscal Impact:

SES has provided a comprehensive report identifying all measures for the project, with a
proposed cost of approximately $18,200,000. The solar panel array portion of the project is
approximately $12,000,000 that will be financed. The City will fund the remaining $6,200,000.
The Fiscal Year 2023/24 budget already includes $1,935,000 appropriation for Park lighting
improvements, the remaining $4,265,000 additional funding will be requested for approval at a
later time: $2,200,000 from Proposition C and $2,065,000 from existing capital reserves.

Project cost per location and per various components is detailed in Attachment 3.

The City will solicit proposals for tax-exempt municipal lease financing of $12,000,000 that will
